# ⬢ STROT

### The open decision compiler

Compile your intent once with an LLM. Then decide on every record forever — classification, scoring, routing — as type-safe JSON with probabilities and confidence, on your own hardware, at zero marginal cost .

Website · Docs · Benchmarks · PyPI

Agents at compile time. Never at runtime.

pip install strot-ai

import strot result = strot . run ( tickets , query = "Triage incoming support tickets into the correct workflow." , action_registry = { "billing_dispute" : "Refunds, invoice corrections, double charges" , "technical_defect" : "Crashes, bugs, broken behavior" , }, llm = "anthropic/claude-opus-4-8" , # used once, on first compile only ) for o in result . outcomes : print ( o [ "action" ], round ( o [ "confidence" ], 2 )) # billing_dispute 0.97 # technical_defect 0.94

The LLM runs once , at compile time. Production is a frozen, self-contained Python artifact: a small local decision model arbitrates every record, nothing is generated, every output is bounded, and low-confidence records abstain instead of guessing.

STROT = Agentic Schema Intent + Compiler & State + Code + Execution + NLU ⟹ JSON Decisions (classification · scoring · routing · typed answers)

## How it works

COMPILE (once per intent + schema) intent + sample ─▶ synthesize ─▶ golden gate ─▶ teacher labels ─▶ calibrate (labels, (your known (annotate (fit the projection, answers must a sample, confidence handlers) pass) once) threshold) │ ▼ frozen artifact (.py) RUNTIME (every record, forever) record ─▶ projection ─▶ decision model ─▶ confidence gate ─▶ typed JSON (compiled) (144M, CPU, (decide or decision ~60 ms) abstain)

## Two surfaces

run() — route each record to an action and execute the compiled handler.

decide() — answer typed questions (choice / score / boolean) per record:

result = strot . decide ( records , questions = { "is_bug_report" : { "type" : "boolean" , "instructions" : "mentions crashes/errors?" }, "customer_sentiment" :{ "type" : "score" , "min" : 1 , "max" : 5 , "instructions" : "1 angry, 5 happy" }, "routing_bucket" : { "type" : "choice" , "options" : [ "billing" , "engineering" , "spam" ]}, }) # → {"booleans": {...}, "scores": {...}, "choices": {...}} with probabilities + confidence

## Measured

Real model (SupersonicLabs/Julia-1, 144M, CPU), real datasets, clean Docker containers:

Reproduce everything: benchmarks/ — with the losses published too.

## What makes it different

- Compile once, decide forever — content-addressed artifact cache; schema drift triggers exactly one recompile.

- Golden-record promotion — artifacts must pass your known answers before they serve.

- Fitted guarantees — temperature scaling + split conformal prediction, baked in: dispatched decisions are wrong ≤ α of all records (marginal); the rest abstain.

- Measured, not guessed — the compiler scores labelings, and can train a distilled head, keeping only what beats the baseline on held-out data.

- 0% structural hallucination — output is selection + computation over your registry; nothing is generated at runtime.

- Model-independent — the decision model is a slot ( nlu= ): local Julia-1 by default, hosted APIs, or any drop-in specialist.

## Install

pip install strot-ai # core: pure stdlib pip install strot-ai[local] # + the local decision model (torch/transformers) pip install strot-ai[hosted] # + openai, for a hosted decision runtime pip install strot-ai[anthropic] # + anthropic, for the synthesizer

Bake the local model into your image for offline production:

RUN pip install strot-ai[local] \ && python -c "import strot; strot.prefetch_nlu(local_dir='/opt/julia-1', install=True)" ENV STROT_NLU_CHECKPOINT=/opt/julia-1

(Never pip install julia — unrelated package.)

## Documentation

DEVELOPERS.md — architecture, compile lifecycle, calibration semantics and caveats, deployment, model swapping, full API reference.

# AI Service Indicators

A community-maintained list of DNS hostnames for generative-AI applications and APIs, for measuring observed AI-service access from DNS, proxy or firewall logs.

Each row maps a hostname pattern to a service, vendor, category and role, so you can tell chat use from API calls, agents, sign-in, CDN, telemetry and plain website visits. Where a vendor publishes the hostname, the row links to that page.

> A DNS lookup shows a device contacted a service, not that anyone submitted a prompt. Report results as observed access, count distinct devices rather than queries, and remember that devices are not people.

## The data

data/ai_services.csv

### Roles

### Confidence

confidence describes the role. A source on a catch-all or hostname row shows that the domain belongs to the vendor, not what each subdomain does. Corrections backed by vendor documentation are especially welcome.

Using role , you can tell, for example, ChatGPT chat ( chatgpt.com , ws.chatgpt.com ) apart from OpenAI API calls ( api.openai.com ), Codex agents ( codex-cloud-backend.chatgpt.com ), and someone reading openai.com or help.openai.com .

No field contains a comma or quote, so any CSV reader, awk -F, , or a SIEM lookup can load the file as-is.

### Matching rules

- Lowercase the queried hostname and strip any trailing dot.

- Try rows in file order ; the first matching row wins. Specific names come before their wildcard catch-alls ( api.openai.com before *.openai.com ).

- A pattern matches the whole hostname: *.chatgpt.com matches ab.chatgpt.com but not fakechatgpt.com or chatgpt.com.example.net . Apex domains are listed separately.

- A hostname matching no row is not in scope.

These are the semantics of a Splunk WILDCARD lookup with max_matches=1 .

## How to interpret results

- Report by role , not by domain. Telemetry and experiment names (for example ab.chatgpt.com ) fire on page load and are often queried by more devices than the app itself. There is no blanket "all openai.com = ChatGPT" rule.

- An API hostname identifies the service contacted, not the application, person, model or billing account behind it. api.anthropic.com , for example, is used by Claude Code as well as by custom applications.

- A usage role shows that a service was in use on a device, not what the person did with it. DNS cannot show whether someone generated an image, ran an agent or only opened the app.

- Some vendor names are reached from other companies' websites. bzr.openai.com , for example, is OpenAI's ad-measurement pixel, embedded in advertisers' sites, and is queried by devices that never use ChatGPT.

- Keep non-usage roles out of usage counts. auth , cdn , telemetry and web names can corroborate activity, but browsers prefetch them, and they are reached by people who never use the product.

- Count distinct devices per service per day or week, not queries. Caching, retries, background refresh and prefetching distort query counts.

- Classify the name the client asked for , not CDN alias (CNAME) targets in the response.

### Coverage gaps

DNS-based measurement misses:

- off-network devices;

- clients using encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT) to outside resolvers;

- locally run models;

- AI features embedded in other SaaS products, which share the host application's hostnames;

- calls made from a vendor's backend.

Some services (OpenRouter, Azure AI Foundry, Bedrock, Vertex AI) front many models, and DNS cannot tell which model was used.

## Using it

Implement the matching rules above. For each pattern, a regex of ^ + the pattern with * replaced by .* (everything else escaped) + $ is enough. In Splunk, load the CSV as a lookup with match_type = WILDCARD(host_pattern) and max_matches = 1 .

On high-volume DNS indexes, filter on indexed terms before classifying: python3 scripts/splunk_terms.py prints a keyword filter that covers every pattern.

## Contributing

New services, endpoints and corrections are welcome. See CONTRIBUTING.md . Every change must pass python3 scripts/validate.py , which also runs automatically on pull requests.

# TenseMem

Memory that knows its tenses. Embedded, deterministic memory that AI agents can safely act on.

One SQLite file. No server required. The model proposes typed facts; the engine decides what is current.

pip install tensemem

from tensemem import FakeExtractor , Memory mem = Memory ( llm = FakeExtractor ()) mem . register_predicate ( "lives_in" ) added = mem . add ( "u1" , "I live in Delhi" ) ctx = mem . context ( user_id = "u1" , min_seq = added . seq , wait = 1.5 ) print ( ctx . text ) # fenced block the model can read print ( ctx . freshness . is_current ) # True once extract finished

FakeExtractor is rule-based and needs no API key. Same API with tensemem[openai] , tensemem[anthropic] , tensemem[ollama] , tensemem[litellm] , or Gemini ( GEMINI_API_KEY in the process environment).

## Why this exists

Similarity search returns both “I live in Delhi” and “I moved to Bangalore” and leaves the model to guess. TenseMem keeps one current value per slot, says whether the read is fresh, and refuses to learn from its own output.

- One current truth per ONE slot. A new city supersedes the old one. History still answers “where did I live before?”

- Every read reports freshness. as_of_seq , pending , is_current . Wait for a message, or see that it is not applied yet.

- No self-echo. Recalled context() is fenced. Extract needs a verbatim quote from the user.

- Corrections stick. correct() restores the displaced value and survives rebuild() with a newer model.

- The engine decides. The LLM emits typed ops. Deterministic rules apply them.

- No infrastructure. Default store is one SQLite file inside your process.

## Delhi, then Bangalore

mem . add ( "u1" , "I live in Delhi" ) mem . set ( user_id = "u1" , predicate = "lives_in" , value = "Bangalore" ) print ( mem . state ( "u1" ). values ) # {"lives_in": "Bangalore"} history = mem . history ( "u1" , predicate = "lives_in" ) # ACTIVE Bangalore, SUPERSEDED Delhi bangalore = next ( f for f in history . facts if f . object == "Bangalore" ) mem . correct ( bangalore . id ) # that move was never true print ( mem . state ( "u1" ). values ) # {"lives_in": "Delhi"}

flowchart LR E[episodes] --> X[extractor proposes ops] X --> R[resolver] R --> F[facts] F --> C["context() + freshness"] C -.->|fence stripped| X

## Architecture

Every surface is an adapter over Memory / AsyncMemory . The model proposes typed ops; resolve() decides mutations; apply() writes one SQLite file. Facts are a rebuildable projection of an append-only episode log.

Editable source: docs/architecture.excalidraw . File map: Architecture .

Do not auto-register unknown predicates, skip keep_ops , or teach the engine from fenced context() text. Those are locked by tests.

## Safe to act (TenseBench)

tensemem bench scores the packaged 101 conversations with FakeExtractor (no network):

Reproduce with tensemem bench . Methodology: TenseBench .

## Inspect

tensemem inspect --user u1 tensemem history --user u1 lives_in tensemem search --user u1 " where did I live "

TenseMem Studio is a local Next.js inspector over tensemem serve (board, memories table, playground, compare, echo). It is not a chatbot. Secrets stay in the serve process environment — never in the Token field. Studio lives in the git checkout, not on PyPI.

git clone https://github.com/tensemem/tensemem.git cd tensemem pip install " tensemem[server] "

Terminal 1 — HTTP:

tensemem --db ./studio.db serve --port 8080

Terminal 2 — Studio:

cd studio && npm install && npm run dev

## Extras

Gemini extract uses GEMINI_API_KEY (or GOOGLE_API_KEY ) in the environment of the process that runs extract. No extra package beyond the server if you use the built-in Gemini adapter.

--token / TENSEMEM_TOKEN is optional bearer auth on HTTP. Bind stays loopback unless you put a TLS proxy in front.

## Status

0.1.0 alpha. The Python API, CLI, REST, MCP, and Studio are usable on a single SQLite file. The default store is SQLite; a second SQL dialect is not shipped. Multi-tenant hosted Studio is not in this tree.

# Tessary

Stop your agents from failing silently in production.

Docs · Self-host · Report an issue · Discussions

Tessary is an open-source reliability platform for AI agents in production. It monitors every trace, detects issues using cheap classifiers, groups related findings into cases, and investigates their root cause using trace and repository evidence.

## Get running

To try it without installing anything, sign up for Tessary Cloud at https://app.tessary.ai . It's free, needs no credit card, and its limits are on the pricing page .

To self-host, paste this into your coding agent:

Self-host Tessary for me by following https://github.com/tessaryai/tessary/blob/main/setup.md

setup.md is written as instructions to an agent: install what's missing, bring every service up, verify the frontend, and hand back the URL.

Prefer to run it yourself? The same install is one command, with nothing cloned and no .env to edit:

docker compose -f oci://docker.io/tessaryai/tessary:compose up -d -y

Either way, open http://localhost when docker compose -p tessary ps reports every service healthy. It needs Docker Engine 26 or newer and Docker Compose v2.34 or newer on the machine. Set up Tessary takes it from there.

Once it's running, instrument your agent so Tessary has traces to watch: see the instrumentation overview .

### 1. Point your agent's traces at it

Send OTLP traces to the endpoint shown during setup and add tessary.call_site.id to spans that invoke a model. Use instrument.md to have a coding agent identify and instrument these call sites.

### 2. Connect the repo (optional)

Connect a GitHub repository under Settings > Git integration and both triage and RCA cite the code that produced the failing traces.

## How it works

- Watch every trace. OTLP over HTTP and gRPC, and SDK push, normalize to the OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* conventions at the edge. PII (personally identifiable information) redaction runs before storage.

- Filter cheaply. Classifiers sweep every trace continuously and open a finding when one fires. The per-trace check stays cheap enough to afford at production volume, which is what makes reading all of it possible instead of sampling. Two classifiers are exceptions, and both are off until you turn them on: frustration scores eligible user messages with a hosted model on your own OpenRouter or TypeSafe key, and groundedness checks answers against their retrieved documents with a public model you run on a Mac with Apple silicon or a GPU instance on AWS, not an LLM call.

- Group into cases. Related findings collapse into one case, surfaced on Triage . An LLM triage step rules whether a finding is a real deviation rather than a legitimate change, and only a finding it rules real becomes a case. Two kinds of finding are ruled when they are filed instead, because their numbers are the claim: a high-confidence secret leak, and a rise in frustrated conversations.

- Explain the case. RCA runs an agentic session over the failing traces and, when a repo is connected, the code itself. It returns a one-sentence summary, the causes it found with the traces behind each, and the checks it ruled out.

- Route it to a human. An alert carries the case to whoever owns it. Tessary explains and hands off. It doesn't open the fix.

## License

Tessary is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 .

## Telemetry

A self-hosted instance sends one anonymous heartbeat to home.tessary.ai at backend start and every 6 hours after. It carries a schema version, an install id, a ping sequence number, a timestamp, the edition, the app version, the host OS family and CPU architecture, install-wide totals of projects, ingested spans, findings, cases, and classifier detections, and the hash of the model price book it holds. On the same schedule it checks home.tessary.ai for a newer price book and downloads it only when the hash has changed. It never carries trace or prompt content, an email address, an org or project name, a hostname, or a retained IP address.

TESSARY_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false

Set that in .env and the instance makes no call to that host, DNS lookups included, and loses nothing: no feature, license check, or in-app behavior depends on the heartbeat reaching us. The field-by-field contract is the telemetry contract .

## Contributing

CONTRIBUTING.md explains how to open an issue or a pull request, how to run the checks locally, and what to expect from review. The documentation map is where to start reading the rest.

## Security

Report a vulnerability privately by emailing security@tessary.ai . See SECURITY.md for what to expect.

# Rembrandt

Stop paying for Adobe. Flush the incrapification.

A free photo editor for macOS, Windows and Linux. No account needed, no subscription, no “we’ve updated our terms” emails.

Download · Self-host · Features · Compare · Build

## Download

All files and checksums: Releases . Builds aren't code-signed yet: on macOS use System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway ; on Windows More info → Run anyway .

## Self-host it

Serve Rembrandt from the computer that holds your photos and edit them in any browser:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thesnarkitecht/rembrandt/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --server

It asks which photo folder to use, starts at login, and prints a private link. Edits are saved next to each photo as XMP; the photos themselves are never changed. Add --lan to reach it from other devices on your network. Linux and macOS; one small dependency-free binary ( server/ ). To update, press Update in the browser (Settings › About); it installs the latest release, checks it against the published SHA-256 sums, and restarts the server.

## Features

- Ask in words : type “warmer and a bit brighter”, “down exposure by ten points”, “shadows +25” or “paste the edits from the previous photo” (Ctrl/⌘ K). A small Rembrandt in dots thinks it over, then makes each change while you watch the sliders move. It runs on your device: a vocabulary, not a language model.

- Edit the photo itself : drag up or down on any part of the picture to lighten or darken that tone, left or right to change that colour; the sliders follow.

- AI looks : Enhance, Relight, Sky, Atmosphere, Sunrays, Skin, Motion and Lens Blur with aperture shapes, from on-device depth and subject maps.

- Refocus : brings back detail in out-of-focus photos, even heavy defocus (regularised deconvolution on the GPU), on the subject or the whole picture.

- Super Resolution : 2× and 4× with real detail, or Restore at the same size for soft photos; runs on the GPU (Metal on Apple silicon).

- AI Denoise : clean high-ISO shots into a new DNG with the same edits, on the GPU.

- Background work that stays out of the way : AI Denoise, Super Resolution and merges run in small GPU slices that pause while you edit, or when you're away, or overnight in a night window you set (Settings › Performance). The queue survives restarts.

- Merge : HDR from brackets, panoramas and focus stacks, each to a RAW-like DNG.

- RAW from 1,000+ cameras, developed on the GPU: tone, colour, curves, grading, dehaze, detail.

- Masks : brush, gradients, colour and tone ranges, AI subject, background, object and depth.

- Remove : heal and clone spots and strokes; Rembrandt picks a matching source for you.

- Lens corrections : the camera's built-in profile from Fujifilm and Sony RAWs, or one of 1,500 lens profiles from Lensfun (distortion, vignetting, chromatic aberration), plus manual distortion and vignetting for any photo. Auto straighten levels horizons.

- On-device AI : Refocus, background replacement. Nothing is uploaded.

- Library : albums, ratings, flags, colour labels, keywords, virtual copies, search, Find similar, sorting, keyboard shortcuts (or Lightroom's), one-click delete with Undo.

- Batch : copy and paste edits to hundreds of photos, batch export, and presets that fit each photo's exposure. Watch a folder to apply a preset and album to new photos as they arrive.

- Share how : a before/after page with a slider, a replay video of the edit, or the recipe inside the exported file so anyone can see (and reuse) how it was edited.

- Bring your photos : folders, Lightroom Classic (edits, keywords, labels, virtual copies, collections, with a report of anything that can't come over) and Lightroom, Google Photos, Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive ( setup ). Export back to them too.

- Open formats : edits are standard XMP, readable by Lightroom and others. Exports keep the camera details and date taken, add your name and copyright, and embed an sRGB profile; location is never written.

- Cloud sync (optional, paid) : turn it on in Settings to sync edits, albums and photos between your computers, the web and your phone. It's the only thing that needs an account, and the only thing that costs money; everything else stays free.

## How it compares

- Lightroom : the everyday editing and library work is here: RAW development, masks (including AI subject, depth and object), healing, presets, lens corrections, HDR and panorama merges, denoise, batch editing, and catalog import. Not here yet: Print, Book, Slideshow, Web and Map modules, face recognition, Adobe's camera profiles, tethered capture (a watched folder covers most tethering apps), and a plugin ecosystem.

- darktable : Rembrandt borrows darktable's central idea, a scene-referred pipeline (edits work on linear light before a tone curve maps it to the screen), which is why highlights recover cleanly. darktable has far more modules and control; Rembrandt aims to be usable in five minutes, with fewer, broader controls and on-device AI. The engine is an independent implementation (see Credits).

- RawTherapee / ART : similar ground to darktable; Rembrandt trades depth of control for speed of use.

- GIMP / Photoshop : different kind of tool. Those are pixel editors for compositing and painting; Rembrandt is a non-destructive RAW developer and library, like Lightroom.

## Your photos aren't locked in

Rembrandt never moves or rewrites your originals. Edits are saved as standard XMP sidecars next to your photos, which Lightroom, darktable and others can read, and Settings › Data & privacy exports a backup of all your edits. If Rembrandt disappeared tomorrow, your library and your edits would still be yours, in open formats.

## How it's built

JavaScript with WebGL2 and WebGPU shaders for the editing engine and on-device AI, in a small Rust ( Tauri ) desktop app. RAW files are decoded by LibRaw (C++, compiled to WebAssembly). Every release is built by GitHub Actions from this repository, with checksums and signed build provenance ( SECURITY.md ).

## Credits

- darktable : the scene-referred workflow Rembrandt's engine is modelled on. An early prototype ported darktable's algorithms; it was replaced by an independent implementation of the published methods (listed in NOTICE.md ) before the code was released.

- LibRaw (RAW decoding), Lensfun (lens profiles), RAWmakase (lens tables, heal and clone), Real-ESRGAN (Super Resolution), KAIR / FFDNet (AI Denoise), MediaPipe (subject, depth and object models). Licences and notices in NOTICE.md .

## Help out

Rembrandt is free and stays free. Star the repo, tell a photographer, report a bug or send a fix.

## Build

npm ci && npx http-server -c-1 . # web app npm run tauri dev # desktop app (Rust + Tauri prerequisites)

# Veda: The Agentic-Native Operating System

Veda is an operating system with a voice agent built in. Say "Hey Veda, switch my wallpaper to the dunes" and it does the work in any application, through the same code as your keyboard and mouse. It asks you first before anything that is hard to undo.

The system is written in Rust and lives in this repository: the UEFI bootloader, a capability-based microkernel, the system services, the window system, the toolkit and the applications. Where a proven, widely used library exists, Veda uses it rather than its own: TCP/IP, TLS and cryptography (smoltcp, rustls, RustCrypto), image codecs (zune, qoi, fast_image_resize) and math (libm, glam, rand). Veda runs on x86-64 PCs and in QEMU.

## Why agentic-native

Operating systems were designed for a person at a keyboard. An assistant added later has to read the screen, imitate clicks or use the few applications that have an API, and the system cannot hold it to anything. In Veda, the agent is a first-class user of the system:

- Part of the system. The agent is a system service, started at boot and restarted if it fails. It sleeps until you say its name, click the ring on the taskbar or press Super+Space .

- Native in every application. Applications declare their actions (typed parameters and a risk level) and report what they show as JSON. The agent calls those actions, which run the same code as the keyboard and mouse: no screen scraping, no simulated clicks. The built-in applications offer more than 70 actions.

- Consent enforced by the system. Every action is routine , sensitive or destructive . The agent service, not the language model, holds the last two until you allow them. Only the desktop shell can answer ( init tells every service which program is calling), so nothing the agent reads in a document can approve anything.

- Real context. Each conversation starts with the time, the open windows, every application's actions, what the agent knows about you and how your last conversation ended. Before acting, it reads the applications' current state.

- Memory you control. It remembers only what you tell it plainly (your name, the people in your life, how you like things done), never its own guesses. The memory stays on your computer, and Settings shows and forgets any part of it.

- Voice first. You can interrupt it at any time. Echo cancellation and an echo gate keep it from hearing itself, and other sound drops 20 dB during a conversation. Asleep, it listens with a voice detector that runs locally, so no audio leaves the computer while nobody speaks.

- The intelligence is a setting. Speech recognition, the language model and the voice come from Deepgram's Voice Agent API, with the audio opted out of Deepgram's model improvement. The model (OpenAI's gpt-4.1-mini by default), the voice and even the agent's name are chosen in Settings.

## How the agent works

- Listening. Asleep, the agent runs a voice detector on the computer. Speech it hears goes to Deepgram's recogniser, with the agent's name as a key term. A sentence that starts or ends with the name ("Hey Veda, …", "…, Veda?") wakes the agent, and the rest of the sentence is its first request.

- Conversation. Waking opens a Deepgram Voice Agent session with the agent's instructions, context and functions. Deepgram handles turn-taking, the language model and the voice; Veda's audio service carries the sound both ways.

- Action. The model calls the agent's 17 functions (windows, files, volume, Wi-Fi, wallpaper, notifications, timers and reminders, memory, the system and its programs) and, through use_app and read_app , every application's actions and state. Each call returns a structured result.

- Consent. A call that needs your OK waits in the agent's window, or in a notification, saying exactly what will happen and to what. It runs only if you allow it within three minutes. Sensitive actions can be allowed for good; destructive ones are asked about every time.

The agent covers the design in full: the protocols, the voice pipeline, consent, memory and testing.

## The operating system

- Microkernel. vkernel handles only isolation, scheduling, memory and IPC: capability handles with rights, channels that carry messages and handles, VMOs, events, futexes and interrupt objects. It supports SMP with x2APIC, tickless timers and XSAVE.

- Supervised services. Drivers, the file system, the window system, audio, networking and the agent are user-space processes. init restarts the window system, the shell, audio, networking and the agent if they crash, so the desktop comes back on its own.

- Linux's drivers in a VM. Veda drives only its disks (virtio-blk, AHCI, NVMe). Linux drives everything else in the driver VM , on Veda's own hypervisor (VMX with EPT, no emulated hardware). Devices go to it whole, their DMA confined and their interrupts remapped by Veda's IOMMU driver. A crashed driver takes down only the VM, which Veda resets and restarts. See the driver VM .

- Desktop. A compositing window manager with server-side decorations, shadows, animations, snapping and an Alt+Tab switcher with live thumbnails. It composes on the GPU with Intel graphics and on the processor elsewhere; once Linux drives the display, every frame is flipped whole at the vertical blank. The shell has a taskbar, a searchable start menu, desktop icons, a calendar and notifications.

- Toolkit. vui is an immediate-mode toolkit: widgets, menus, dialogs, vector icons and anti-aliased text in Inter and JetBrains Mono. Every vui application is agent-compatible.

- 3D graphics. OpenGL ES 3.0 with GLSL ES 1.00 and 3.00, in Rust ( vgl , vglsl ), every call checked as the specification requires. It renders on the GPU through Mesa in the driver VM (Intel's iris; virgl on the host's GPU under QEMU), or on a multi-threaded software renderer. Interceptor shows it off, full screen: a bay city with its traffic, physically based lighting, shadows, bloom and 4x multisampling.

- Networking. A network service with IPv4 and IPv6, DHCP, DNS, TCP, UDP and ICMP, and a Wi-Fi service that joins WPA2, WPA3 and open networks with management frame protection, remembers them, reconnects and roams. Linux's drivers only move frames and never see a password. Applications get TLS 1.3 and 1.2 from vtls , with certificates checked against Mozilla's roots. See Networking .

- Audio. A mixing service with echo-cancelled recording and ducking, built for the agent's conversations as much as for music.

- Video. FFmpeg and dav1d, ported to Veda, decode the common formats (AV1, VP9, H.264, HEVC and more) in a sandboxed process that reaches nothing but the file it is given: a damaged file that crashes or hangs it costs a moment, not the video. Pictures come through shared memory and are shown in time with the sound, timed to the screen's refresh. See Architecture .

- Storage. The home directory has its own disk. It is saved half a second after changes stop, alternating between two checksummed slots, so an interrupted save never damages the previous one. The agent's memory and key live in a private directory that only the agent can open.

- C and GCC. The image includes GCC 16, binutils and musl: write a C program in the Terminal, compile it and run it, in QEMU or on a PC. C programs are static executables whose system calls go to vposix , a POSIX layer in Rust. A cross compiler also builds C and C++ programs for Veda on the development machine. See C on Veda .

## Applications

Every application is agent-compatible: what you can do with the mouse and keyboard, the agent can do too.

## Screenshots

Every screenshot is 1280x800. They are taken in QEMU by cargo xtask script docs/screenshots.vts , with the agent talking to a stand-in for Deepgram. Interceptor's is taken at 1920x1200 by cargo xtask script docs/interceptor.vts --resolution 1920x1200 and scaled down.

## Quick start

### Requirements

Veda is built on an x86-64 PC with Linux.

- Rust , stable. rust-toolchain.toml makes rustup install the extra targets on first use, and Rust's own linker ( rust-lld ) links everything.

- QEMU and the OVMF UEFI firmware (on Debian and Ubuntu: qemu-system-x86 , qemu-system-gui , qemu-system-modules-opengl and ovmf ), with access to /dev/kvm .

- For the driver VM: the build tools for Linux, a cross compiler and Mesa (on Debian and Ubuntu: build-essential , bc , curl , rsync , m4 , flex , bison , meson , ninja-build , libgmp-dev , libmpfr-dev , libmpc-dev , python3-mako and python3-packaging ), and KVM's nested virtualization ( kvm_intel nested=1 ). See the driver VM .

- Optional: a Deepgram API key for the agent, and your distribution's build tools for the C toolchain, which cargo xtask toolchain builds once (see C on Veda ), with nasm for the video decoders it builds too.

Check the environment:

cargo xtask doctor

### Build and run

First, build the driver VM's Linux (its kernel, a cross compiler and Mesa), which takes a while. Without it, Veda boots with no keyboard, mouse, sound or network.

cargo xtask linux

Then build and run Veda:

cargo xtask run

This builds every component, writes target/veda/veda.img and boots it in a QEMU window at 1920x1080. The first build also renders the sample pictures, music and videos. Later builds are incremental.

Videos plays videos with FFmpeg and dav1d, which the C toolchain builds (it needs nasm ). Build it once, and the images built after it include the decoder:

cargo xtask toolchain

cargo xtask run --resolution 1280x800 --smp 4 --memory 2048 cargo xtask run --cmdline " run=editor " cargo xtask run --net wifi

run=NAME starts /system/bin/NAME.exe after boot. By default the machine reaches the Internet through a wired card on QEMU's NAT. --net wifi gives it a Wi-Fi radio instead, and starts airsim , a simulated Wi-Fi environment whose networks ("Veda Home", "Veda WPA3", ...) lead to the Internet with the password veda-wifi ; --net both gives it both. cargo xtask help lists every command and option.

### A real PC, from a USB stick

cargo xtask iso

This writes target/veda/veda.iso , a live system. To start it:

- Write it to a USB stick with Rufus (partition scheme GPT, target system UEFI, ISO mode) or with any image writer.

- In the PC's firmware settings, turn on VT-x and VT-d and turn off Secure Boot (Veda's loader is not signed).

- Start the PC from the stick in UEFI mode, usually from the boot menu (F12, F11 or Esc at power-on).

Veda runs from memory and starts no disk driver, so it never reads or writes the PC's disks. Its home directory lasts until the PC is turned off. To try the stick in QEMU first, run cargo xtask run --live .

The stick keeps a log of every start in VEDA/LOGS , one numbered folder per start (the newest has the highest number): VEDA.TXT from Veda and LINUX.TXT from the driver VM. They are synced every second, so even a start that shows nothing can be diagnosed on another computer.

Linux's drivers in the driver VM support:

Without VT-x and VT-d, Veda drives only the disks (with VT-x alone, PS/2 keyboards and mice too). USB disks, the stick included, are left alone. Status shows how far each device class has come. To try USB input or HD Audio in QEMU:

cargo xtask run --input usb cargo xtask run --sound hda

## Talking to Veda

- Open Settings → Agent and add your Deepgram API key. The agent's name, voice, language model, listening and memory are on the same page.

- Say "Hey Veda" , click the ring at the right of the taskbar or press Super+Space .

- Talk naturally and interrupt whenever you like. Say goodbye when you are done, and it goes back to sleep.

Veda uses the PC's microphone and speakers, under QEMU too. It speaks English only for now. Deepgram bills every minute of conversation; asleep, only the short recognitions that check for its name are billed, at most ten minutes an hour.

Things to ask:

- "Switch my wallpaper to the dunes."

- "Play Neon Horizon."

- "Write a shopping list with eggs, milk and coffee."

## What is this?

cliproxy-rs is a small server you run on your own computer. It lets your coding tools, such as Claude Code, Codex CLI or Cursor, use the AI subscriptions and API keys you already have, like a Claude Max plan or a ChatGPT plan, through one local address. A dashboard built into it shows which accounts work, how much of each plan's limits is left, and how to connect each tool.

It is a Rust rewrite of CLIProxyAPI . It reads the same config.yaml and the same account files, so you can switch between the two in either direction.

## Why would I want it?

- You pay for Claude and ChatGPT plans and want Claude Code, Codex CLI and your editor to share them, with the 5-hour and weekly limits of every account on one screen.

- You have several Claude or Codex accounts and want requests spread across them, or moved to the next account when one reaches its limit.

- A tool speaks only one API: the proxy translates between the Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini formats, so an OpenAI-only tool can use a Claude account and the other way round.

- You run CLIProxyAPI and want a smaller, faster-starting binary with the dashboard built in.

# Can AI draw San Francisco from memory?

In 2023, Gurnee and Tegmark showed that you can read the latitude and longitude of places straight out of a language model's activations. So there is a map in there somewhere. We wanted to see it.

We gave six AI models 41,526 points of San Francisco and asked what is at each one: water, a park, a building, a street or something else. They answered from memory, with no maps and no internet, and we checked every answer against OpenStreetMap.

The best models know San Francisco like a tourist with a good memory. They put the coastline, Golden Gate Park and the Presidio in the right place and get the street grid wrong. Paying five times more bought the same score, and thinking harder did not find the streets. Jev, a model from TypeSafe that we asked one point at a time, put the Marina underwater and was only 37% sure of its answers there.

The code, every answer and the answer keys are open. Three commands rebuild the scores, costs and figures without an API key ( run it yourself ).

Jump to: the whole city · the Marina · one block, medium against high · what broke · how precise this is

## What we asked

Every chat model got the same question, 100 points at a time, in random order:

> You are taking part in a map-knowledge test about San Francisco, California. Answer from your own knowledge only. Below are 100 locations in San Francisco, in no particular order, as WGS84 latitude, longitude: 1. 37.80241, -122.44853 ... For each location give one letter for what is at that exact spot: W = water (bay, ocean, lake or pond), P = park, lawn, trees or other green open space, H = inside a building, S = on a street (roadway or sidewalk), O = anything else (parking lot, plaza, beach or empty lot).

You are taking part in a map-knowledge test about San Francisco, California. Answer from your own knowledge only.

Below are 100 locations in San Francisco, in no particular order, as WGS84 latitude, longitude: 1. 37.80241, -122.44853 ...

For each location give one letter for what is at that exact spot: W = water (bay, ocean, lake or pond), P = park, lawn, trees or other green open space, H = inside a building, S = on a street (roadway or sidewalk), O = anything else (parking lot, plaza, beach or empty lot).

We tested two models from each of the big three, at low, medium and high reasoning:

We also asked two things that are not chat models, one point at a time: Jev by TypeSafe, and OpenAI's Decisions API, which runs GPT-6 Luna. Both answer a multiple-choice question and return a probability for each choice, so they seemed a natural fit for "which of these five is it?"

There are three maps:

- All of San Francisco, a point every 100 m. 15,846 points. At this spacing a point lands on a street or a building by chance, so we score it as water, park or everything else.

- Crissy Field, the Palace of Fine Arts and the Marina, a point every 10 m. 23,180 points and all five classes. We slid a box this size over the whole city, and of 236 positions this one has the 4th most even mix of water, parks, buildings and streets. We took it over the top three (Ocean Beach, Lands End and Hunters Point) because it puts Crissy Field, the Palace of Fine Arts and the Marina's grid in one box.

- A 500 x 500 m piece of the Marina street grid, a point every 10 m. 2,500 points at medium and at high reasoning, to see if more thinking finds the streets.

## San Francisco at 100 m

Right is the share of points with the right answer. mIoU is fairer when the classes are uneven: for each class, take the points where the model and the map agree and divide by the points where either of them says that class, then average over water, park and everything else. The table is sorted by mIoU.

Every model draws its best map at high reasoning. Gemini 4 Argon stays flat from low to medium, because it only starts reasoning at high. Claude Fable 5.1 costs the most at low and medium and lands behind the OpenAI models and Gemini 4 Argon on mIoU at every level.

At high reasoning, Gemini 4 Argon, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra are within a point of each other, which is a tie, and Astra costs five times more than the other two. GPT-6.1 Sol gets 83% at medium for $4.61.

Argon reached the top only after we re-sent the 4 of its 159 requests that came back empty. On denser maps it breaks much more often (see When the models broke ).

The good maps all have the coastline, Golden Gate Park, the Presidio and Lake Merced. Small parks are hit and miss: the best park score is 0.45. Jev draws a box, with water around the edge and everything else inside, which still beats answering "everything else" everywhere. The Decisions API calls 53% of the city a park.

## The Marina at 10 m

All five classes count here. GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 put the Palace of Fine Arts lagoon in the right place, and Astra and Sol put the Palace building next to it. Fable draws the Marina's long east-west streets as stripes across the whole map.

Claude Opus 5.5 does not believe in streets. It calls 3% of the Marina a street, against 21% in reality, and paints the grid as one big building. That gets it the most points right and the lowest street score of any chat model.

Fable, Astra and Sol score 0.19-0.21 on streets here, against 0.11-0.14 if their own answers were shuffled at random. That looks like knowing which parts of the map are dense grid and which are park.

Jev puts the Marina underwater: 84% of its answers here are water. It was not sure, though. Jev gives a probability for each of the five answers, and the one it picked got 37% on average, against 20% for a blind guess. It was as sure of its wrong answers as of its right ones. The Decisions API's answers were split between water and park, and it was no different: 41% on average, right or wrong.

## Medium against high reasoning on one Marina block

To see whether the models know where single streets run, we took a 500 x 500 m piece of the Marina, 46% buildings and 33% streets, and asked every model at medium and at high reasoning.

High reasoning adds 0.01-0.03 to the street score and costs up to 3.6 times as much (Gemini 4 Argon aside: 48 times as much, for answers on 8% of the points). No model draws the grid at either level. The chance column shows what each model would score if we shuffled its own answers around the block, keeping how often it says "street". Only GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol beat that, by 0.04-0.09, which is a thin margin on 25 requests. Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5 and both Geminis score about what they would by putting the same number of streets in random places.

## When the models broke

Gemini 4 Argon thinks itself out of room. At high reasoning it thinks for about 15,000 tokens per request on the city map. On the dense Marina block it thinks for about 30,000, even when we send it only 10 points. Its output limit is 32,768 tokens, thinking included, so 10-point requests just fit. Redoing the block that way would have cost about $75, so we left the hole.

GPT-6.1 Sol at high can think for up to half an hour per request. After OpenAI's Batch API stalled, we sent the rest through the regular API, and 11 requests outlasted our 30-minute connection limit. OpenAI's background mode, which runs the request on their side and lets you check back later, finished all 11.

In early tests, models asked for 100 letters in a row sometimes wrote 90 or 101. So every answer is numbered ("17:H"), and a missing or extra letter cannot shift the rest.

Apart from Gemini 4 Argon high on the block, every run answered 100% of its points.

## How precise is this?

We ran GPT-6.1 Sol medium and Gemini 4 Argon low on the city map a second time. 12% and 11% of points changed between water, park and everything else (29% and 25% with all five classes), but the scores moved by less than half a point: 83.4% to 83.7% and 80.1% to 79.7%. So both scores held while single points flipped.

We also asked Jev and the Decisions API about every point a second time, to keep their probabilities. The Decisions API gave the same answers both times. Jev changed 9% of its answers on the city map and under 1% elsewhere, and its scores held.

The 95% ranges in results/summary.json come from resampling the requests. They are about ±0.5-0.8 points on the city map, so treat models within a point of each other as tied. On the small block they are about ±3 points.

OpenStreetMap is the answer key, so its mistakes count against the models. A point counts as a street if it is within 5-12 m of a street centreline, depending on the type of road. Freeways and footpaths do not count as streets, and private yards, parking lots and plazas land in "other".

Different wording, points in order instead of shuffled, or fewer points per request would change the numbers. Before this setup we asked for whole drawings of each block and for small grids of points. The drawings had seams where blocks met, and the grids came back with whole rows of the same letter, so we switched to shuffled points. We did not tune the setup on the scores.

## How we did it

- Points. A grid over each map, shuffled once with a fixed seed and cut into requests of 100 points. Jev and the Decisions API answer one point per request.

- Asking. Anthropic and OpenAI through their Batch APIs at half price, Gemini through the regular API. One try per request, except where the table above says otherwise: we asked empty Gemini 4 Argon high answers again (on the block we stopped after 24 retries in a row failed), and OpenAI requests a stalled batch never returned went through the regular API.

- Answer key. OpenStreetMap, downloaded on 18 October 2026. A point is water if it is in the sea, a lake or a pond; else a building if it is inside a building footprint; else a street if it is close to a street centreline; else a park; else other.

- Scoring. The share of points right, and mean IoU over the classes. A point with no answer stays out of "right" but lowers mIoU.

## Run it yourself

uv sync uv run python -m sfmap download # our answers and answer keys, into data/ uv run python -m sfmap score # results/summary.json uv run python -m sfmap figures # figures/ uv run pytest # tests

To ask the models yourself, set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , OPENAI_API_KEY , GEMINI_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_API_KEY , then:

uv run python -m sfmap reference # download OpenStreetMap, build the answer keys uv run python -m sfmap run sf100 # or marina10, block10 uv run python -m sfmap collect # when the batches finish uv run python -m sfmap retry block10 argon high # re-send Gemini requests that came back empty uv run python -m sfmap background sf100 sol high # OpenAI requests a stalled batch never returned uv run python -m sfmap background sf100 sol medium --rerun # a whole second run uv run python -m sfmap references sf100 --rerun # Jev and the Decisions API again, with probabilities

## Who we are

We are VOYGR . We build APIs that tell AI agents which places exist, whether they are open and what they offer. This started as a quick question and got out of hand.

## Models propose. Yana decides. Humans stay in charge.

Yana is the control plane between an AI and real power. A model can say what it wants to do. Yana decides whether that is allowed, and a person can always stop it.

Model proposes an action | Authority is this agent allowed to ask? | Capability what exact power is this? (a small, fixed set) | Policy may it happen now? rules first, then a human | Executor performs only the permitted operation

Any model goes through the same path: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, or one running on your own machine. Skills teach an agent how to work; only a capability can grant permission to act.

## System structure

Live means shipped and in use. In development means real code exists but is not feature-complete. Experimental means opt-in and not independently verified.

yana-rt has 40 subcommands. Zero Python dependency. This is the source-defined count across feature builds, including feature-gated ones.

core/ ├── hooks/ # 66 PreToolUse / PostToolUse / Stop hooks (63 shell, 3 JavaScript) ├── rules/ # 71 rules, most are guidance the agent applies; hooks enforce a subset ├── agents/ # 100 specialist agents ├── skills/ # 2,026 skills ├── commands/ # 170 Claude Code slash commands └── config/ └── core-lock.json # SHA-256 manifest — 287 core files pinned

These counts are derived from the filesystem by core/scripts/check_counts.py , which CI runs, so they should not drift from the tree.

## Yana Studio

One window for the things you switch between when working with AI on a project. Studio talks to the model only through yana-rt ; it never calls a provider from the UI layer.

- Files and editor: open a real folder, search filenames across it, edit with CodeMirror. Files up to 8 MiB are editable; larger ones open as read-only 256 KiB windows. Saves detect outside changes before overwriting.

- Terminals: real PTY sessions in tabs, or a grid of up to 12.

- Git: read-only status, worktrees and diffs. Stage and commit are deliberately not AI tools.

- Chat: streamed through yana-rt , multiple saved conversations, stop button, approval prompts, token usage.

- Models: all 19 providers (13 cloud, 6 local) plus a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint. A local manager detects 9Router, Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, TurboFieldfare and AirLLM. API keys go to Rust over stdin and are stored encrypted with the OS keystore, never in workspace files.

- Tasks: create, list, depend and drop tasks against the real yana-rt task store. Marking done requires evidence, and blocked is always computed by the runtime.

- Design canvas: native canvas with 22 components, phone and desktop screens, layers, undo/redo, and guarded AI proposals.

- Governance telemetry: what was allowed, what was blocked, and why.

Not built yet: device registry, agent sessions screen, mobile pairing, SSH/Docker execution, permission-lease UI, signed auto-update. The per-screen status is in tools/yana-studio/SCREEN-STATUS.md .

Download from the latest release or yana.vutam.link .

Each release lists its own assets, so check that your platform is there, and verify against SHA256SUMS when provided. There is no Linux ARM build. The macOS build is ad-hoc signed and not notarized (no Apple Developer membership yet), so Gatekeeper warns on first launch; docs/MACOS_INSTALL.md shows the two official ways to open it.

Build from source (Node 24+ and a C++ toolchain for node-pty ):

cd tools/yana-studio npm ci && npm run rebuild npm run stage:runtime -- /absolute/path/to/yana-rt npm start

## Runtime: yana-rt

A single Rust binary that owns the turn loop and the authority check for every client, so Studio, the CLI and MCP do not each reimplement permission logic.

- 19 providers: anthropic, openai, gemini, groq, deepseek, openrouter, xai, novita, nvidia, minimax, glm, huggingface, 9router, kimi (cloud), and ollama, lmstudio, llamacpp, turbofieldfare, airllm (local). The canonical list is src/model/catalog.rs ; a contract test keeps Studio in sync with it.

- Failover: typed provider errors, fallback providers and credential-pool rotation.

- State: SQLite session store with full-text search, per-profile state, crash recovery, and shadow-git checkpoints with rollback.

- Capability tools: file read/patch, command execution under validation, MCP client over stdio, web.search through a checked HTTPS layer, and a read-only LSP client.

- Optional features: mcp , lsp , pty-bridge , Discord remote adapter. They are off in the default build.

Remaining work on the runtime is tracked in CURRENT-MILESTONE.md . At the time of writing: unifying every client on one capability executor, and running local-model tool calling against a real local model rather than a mock.

## Giám Thị

An independent watcher that runs outside any AI session, from the operating system's own scheduler: launchd on macOS, a systemd timer on Linux, Task Scheduler on Windows, every 6 hours.

- It compares the repo against a baseline commit a human approved, over the files that control enforcement: hook settings for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, CI workflows, core/rules , core/gates , core/hooks , core/scripts and src/guard .

- On drift it writes GIAMTHI_HALT.lock . A hook that runs first on every tool call then denies everything while the lock exists.

- Only a person deleting the lock clears it. Neither the hook, the watcher nor any environment variable can.

- Manage it with yana-ai giamthi install | status | repair | uninstall .

It is opt-in. Because it runs on a schedule, there is a window of up to 6 hours between a change and the halt. Codex fires PreToolUse only for shell commands, so Yana also checks the lock on SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit for Codex.

## Harness adapters

Details and switching commands: adapters/README.md .

## Command line

pip install yana-ai # Python CLI yana-ai install # add Yana's hooks and rules to your repo yana-ai doctor . # check that everything is wired cargo install yana-rt # native runtime, no Python needed

Needs Python 3.11+ (or Rust), Git, and one supported harness. All CLI commands are in COMMANDS.md . The 170 Claude Code slash commands ( /plan , /verify , /code-review and others) live in core/commands/ and run inside a session. Yana is not published to npm, see VERSIONING.md .

## What protects you, and where it stops

- Audit log: hash-chained, so editing or deleting a line is detectable ( core/scripts/verify-audit-chain.sh ). It is tamper-detectable, not tamper-proof.

- Core-lock: a SHA-256 manifest detects changed, deleted or injected files in core/ . It proves the tree matches the lock file, not that a human reviewed the change: whoever can edit core/ can also regenerate the lock. Giám Thị is the independent check for that.

- Human gate: force-push, publish, deploy and delete need confirmation in the current session; earlier approval does not carry over.

- Giám Thị: opt-in, runs outside any AI session, and on a finding locks every later tool call until a person removes the lock. It is periodic, not instant.

- Rules versus hooks: most files in core/rules describe behaviour the agent applies to itself. Only what is wired into a hook is enforced. There is no code-signing pipeline.

- Limits: guard-destructive.sh matches command strings, not a full shell parse, so a deliberately crafted command can slip past it. Antigravity is advisory, and Cursor does not screen MCP calls. Browser-only web deployments without the Rust runtime are not fully governed. Details: known limitations .

## Versioning

Three axes, each with its own number and registry: the product (not distributed), yana-rt on crates.io, and the yana-ai Python package on PyPI. Apps under tools/ ship through GitHub Releases with their own tags ( studio-v* for Studio). The numbers are deliberately not repeated here, since they go stale. See VERSIONING.md .

# Unterm

The terminal AI agents can drive.

If Unterm is useful to you, a ⭐ on GitHub helps other people find it.

Cross-platform terminal (macOS / Linux / Windows) built on Unterm's native next-core terminal engine, with one design bet: the terminal itself is controllable from the outside by any AI agent over MCP. Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Aider, your own scripts — they all get the same JSON-RPC surface ( 152 authenticated methods plus auth.login ) to spawn shells, run commands, read pane state, capture screenshots, record sessions, and run the Agent Cockpit. (Theme, language and unterm.conf are not on MCP; they are set through Web Settings, unterm-cli , or the file.)

Since v0.68 the terminal is also something an orchestrator can govern rather than merely call: it publishes what it can do and how dangerous each capability is, works under leases that expire and cannot be replayed, keeps agents inside workspaces that cannot see each other, and can hand you an evidence bundle for a task that somebody who was not there can verify.

Since v0.55 the relationship runs both ways: agents drive the terminal from outside, and the terminal is an Agent Cockpit for the agents running inside it — live per-pane agent state, a waiting-first Inbox, fleets of N agents on one task in N isolated git worktrees, and a Review page to diff / merge / roll back what they produced.

The other 2026 terminals each pick a different side: Warp embeds AI inside a closed cloud (Oz), Ghostty stays out of your way and lets you bring your own tools, iTerm2 is Mac-only. Unterm picks the third side — terminal as MCP-controllable surface, deliberately keep AI generation out of the terminal, let external agents grip it through the API, and give the human one cockpit to run them all from.

Practical implications:

- Every Unterm window starts a local MCP server (line-delimited JSON-RPC over TCP) and a local HTTP settings server (Web Settings page) on auto-allocated ports. Both are auth-token gated, both are 127.0.0.1-only, no cloud round trip.

- Settings live in the browser , not the terminal. Cell-grid TUIs can't deliver modern form UX (no proper text inputs, no live preview, no color picker). The in-terminal ▼ menu holds quick actions and links out to the Web Settings page — configuration itself happens in the browser.

- 9 languages out of the box : en / 简体中文 / 繁體中文 / 日本語 / 한국어 / Deutsch / Français / Italiano / हिन्दी. Auto-detects from system locale, can be overridden in Web Settings or via unterm-cli lang set <code> .

- Multi-instance discovery : every running Unterm process owns one NATO-named instance (alpha, bravo, charlie…) and writes its ports + auth token to ~/.unterm/instances/<name>.json . Agents that drive several windows at once enumerate that directory.

- Cross-platform parity is a correctness property : if a feature works on Windows but bails on macOS or Linux, that's a bug, not "not supported yet."

- Subtraction over decoration : no AI chat overlay inside the terminal and no cloud dependency for core operation. Proxy settings auto-detect the system by default and also support explicit HTTP/SOCKS overrides, node pools, rotation, and Clash/mihomo controllers. Finder integration on macOS uses the native Finder right-click extension and Services.

The GUI and terminal runtime now use Unterm's native next-core engine. The repository still carries selected upstream components and attribution where they remain dependencies, but WezTerm mux/window state is no longer the product kernel.

## Agent Cockpit

Run Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, or Aider in any pane and Unterm sees them — no configuration, no wrapper. Five pillars, all local:

- Agent state engine — every pane's agent and its state (working / waiting-for-you / idle / done), read from OSC progress + title signals, process fingerprints, and optional official hooks. Tab badges + a cross-window tally chip in the top bar.

- Inbox ( Ctrl+Shift+A ) — every agent that's waiting for you in one queue, longest-waiting first. Enter jumps to the pane; one keystroke later you've answered its prompt.

- Fleet — one task × N agents × N isolated git worktrees ( ../<repo>.fleet/ ), one tab each. Same agent ×3 for throughput, or claude,codex,gemini for a bake-off.

- Review — agents get checkpointed before they touch a repo (dangling-commit snapshots; nothing touches your HEAD or index). A Web Review page shows per-member diffs with squash-merge (stops at staged — the commit stays yours), discard, and rollback. Since v0.57, Review also verifies each member (inferred or explicit validation command), ranks members by verification + change size, gates merge on a passing run, and can retry a failed member in its existing worktree.

- Everything scriptable — the cockpit itself is MCP + CLI: agent.status , cockpit.inbox , fleet.launch , review.merge … an orchestrating agent can run fleets and review diffs with no human in the chair.

unterm-cli agent status # who's running where, in what state unterm-cli agent inbox # who's waiting for you unterm-cli agent enable-hooks # exact state via official hooks (merge-only, backed up) unterm-cli fleet launch --agents claude,codex " fix the flaky auth test " unterm-cli review verify --fleet < id > --member 1 # run the member's validation unterm-cli review list && unterm-cli review open # ranked diffs in the browser

Full docs: unterm.app/docs/agent-cockpit .

## Install

Pre-built artifacts are published on GitHub Releases:

https://github.com/zhitongblog/unterm/releases

### macOS

Double-click Unterm-macos-<version>.dmg , then drag Unterm.app onto the Applications shortcut. The DMG is signed with a Developer ID and Apple- notarized, so Gatekeeper opens it on first launch without warnings.

Finder integration is bundled in the DMG. After the first launch, Finder's right-click menu can show Open in Unterm for folders and files; if macOS doesn't refresh the extension immediately, run Repair Finder Integration.app from the DMG once.

### Linux (Debian / Ubuntu)

sudo apt install ./unterm- < version > .deb unterm

Other distros — use the AppImage:

chmod +x Unterm- < version > -x86_64.AppImage ./Unterm- < version > -x86_64.AppImage

### Windows

Run the MSI installer; it places unterm.exe in Program Files\Unterm and creates a Start Menu shortcut.

## What's new

- v0.68 — A terminal something else can govern. Unterm now hosts CLI agents as sessions rather than shelling out and waiting for an exit code ( agent_session.* : what it said, what it asked to run, how it ended, with your own task ids carried through untouched). It can lease a browser from Unzoo and be leased from in turn — terminal.manifest publishes what this terminal can do and how dangerous each family is, taken from the same table the gateway refuses by. Approvals can finally be answered: Settings shows what an agent is waiting on, with "allow once / for this task / always". Workspaces are roots that cannot see each other, and a shell that cd s out stops being inside. The audit trail is hash-chained, so an edit to it disagrees with the next line. unterm-cli provider | scope | artifact | evidence | system — 46 new MCP methods (149 total at the time; 152 today).

- v0.57 — Fleet verification loop + new brand mark. Review now verifies each fleet member automatically (Cargo / Go / npm / pnpm / yarn / Python / Maven / Gradle / .NET inferred, or your own command), ranks members by verification and change size, gates squash-merge on a passing run (audited force override), and retries failed members in their existing worktree without losing work — review.verify / fleet.retry over MCP + CLI. The sidebar gains repository-grouped navigation with always-on fuzzy search. Every logo surface moves to the new command-loop mark.

- v0.55 — Agent Cockpit. The terminal now sees the agents inside it: live per-pane state with tab badges and a cross-window tally, the waiting-first Agent Inbox ( Ctrl+Shift+A ), fleets running one task across N agents in N isolated worktrees, and a Review page with checkpoints, diffs, rollback, and squash-merge. 12 new MCP methods, 3 new CLI families.

- v0.54 — 2.8× faster cold start (~780ms → ~280ms) via five startup-path wins, and no more CPU core burned on Windows output floods (~91% → ~4%); MCP stays responsive mid-flood.

- v0.53 — Composer + Git panel. A prompt queue ( Ctrl+Shift+J ) that runs batched prompts into an agent pane with smart auto-advance through confirmation prompts, and a read-only Git status panel ( Ctrl+Shift+G ).

- v0.52 — More agents out of the box. Kimi Code CLI and Trae Agent join the baked manifest (7 agent CLIs total); reworked per-frame paint paths; steadier Windows clipboard and window sizing.

## Documentation

The full Unterm docs live at https://unterm.app/docs/ :

- Agent Cockpit — agent state engine, Inbox, Fleet, Review: run and supervise CLI agents from one terminal

- Agent integration — how to drive Unterm from Claude Code / Cursor / Aider / your own client

- Agent recipes — copy-paste patterns for common agent-drives-terminal workflows

- Product roadmap — what is being built now and what comes later

- Product requirements — complete product scope, functional requirements, MCP/CLI coverage, and acceptance criteria

- Detailed product planning — Chinese execution plan covering user scenarios, version roadmap, priorities, validation, and next-core migration

- Next-core product plan — staged plan to stabilize the current engine while building Unterm's own terminal core

- Next-core technical architecture — Chinese architecture plan for replacing the WezTerm core without growing into a larger terminal monolith

- MCP reference — every JSON-RPC method, parameters, return shape

- Multi-instance — NATO names, instances directory, picking the right window

- Identity profiles — one window per identity. Bind GitHub / AWS / npm / OpenAI tokens, git identity, SSH key routing all at once. CLI + MCP.

- CLI reference — unterm-cli subcommands, flags, exit codes

- Configuration — every file under ~/.unterm/

- Config file reference — every key in unterm.conf , including [env] and [keys]

- Architecture — what we forked from WezTerm and why

This README is the short version. The site is the long version.

## Features

- GPU-accelerated rendering on all three platforms through wgpu: Metal on macOS, Direct3D 12 on Windows and Vulkan on Linux. If the hardware path fails, Unterm tries OpenGL, then the same two in software (WARP on Windows), and on Windows finally Vulkan — so a machine with no usable graphics driver still opens a window. UNTERM_GPU_BACKEND=dx12|vulkan|gl|metal pins one backend.

- Pictures in the terminal — the kitty graphics protocol, iTerm2 inline images ( OSC 1337 File= ) and sixel, so chafa , img2sixel , viu , timg and unterm-cli imgcat show the image itself. Pictures scroll with their text, stay in the scrollback, are clipped at pane edges and keep to the screen (main or alternate) they were drawn on. screen.images / unterm-cli session images list them for agents.

- MCP server on 127.0.0.1:<auto-port> (default 19876) — line-delimited JSON-RPC over TCP, loopback-only and auth-token gated. It exposes 152 authenticated methods plus auth.login ; meta.surface (or unterm-cli reference ) returns the authoritative live inventory in one call.

- Agent Cockpit — per-pane agent state, waiting-first Inbox, worktree fleets, checkpoint + review. See the section above.

- Governed agent work — one gateway every door goes through (MCP, CLI, brain, workflow, raw PTY write), capability leases with expiry and replay protection, workspaces that cannot see each other, a hash-chained audit trail, and evidence bundles somebody else can verify. # More Space

A chalkboard and an avatar for any terminal agent. It shows its plan, its progress and its questions while it works.

## What it is

More Space is a desktop app with a real terminal floating over an endless chalkboard. Run any agent in that terminal (Claude Code, Codex, or anything else that can run shell commands) and it finds a command there that lets it:

- write and draw on the board: text, checklists, flow diagrams, pinned notes and photos, chalk links between them, circles, underlines and scribbles;

- be someone : an avatar you choose from a cast of characters, each with its own moods, look and voice;

- ask you things : choices, several answers, written answers or a scale, right on the board, and wait for your click;

- steer what you see : frame what it is explaining, or the whole board.

The command exists only inside the app's terminals and talks only to the window that opened them. Nothing is installed in your system, and nothing is written into your project.

## Getting started

- Download the app for your system from Releases (macOS: .dmg for Apple silicon or Intel; Windows: the Setup .exe ; Linux: .AppImage or .deb ).

- Open it and choose a project folder.

- The empty board shows a short instruction with a Copy button. Paste it to your agent in the terminal below; it will start by learning the board.

### Unsigned builds

Builds are not signed yet. The first time:

- macOS : open it once; when macOS says it is from an unidentified developer, go to System Settings → Privacy & Security and choose Open Anyway (on older macOS, right-click the app and choose Open ). Or run xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/More Space.app" . The 0.1.0 build says "damaged" instead: it was not signed at all; the command above opens it.

- Windows : SmartScreen may warn about an unknown publisher; choose More info , then Run anyway .

## What the agent can do

Everything starts from the command with no arguments; each level explains the next, and more-space --all lists everything at once. more-space guide explains the board in one screen.

Several commands can go in one call, one per line: more-space - <<'EOF' … EOF in a Unix shell, or @' … '@ | more-space - in PowerShell. Every write answers with the cells it really covers, and warns when it lands on something else.

The avatar also lives along by itself:

- the terminal : busy while the program keeps printing, "Done" when it goes quiet, and calling you when the program rings the bell or sends a notification;

- the branch : it notices files changing as git sees them (an edit, a new or deleted file, an undone edit, a commit) and reacts in its own moods. Ignored files, like dependencies and builds, never count.

## Characters, sound and handwriting

- Characters : Mochi (the default, a plump pixel spirit), Chalky, Penguin, Owl, Robot, Cat, Cowboy, Samurai, Viking, Astronomer and Anime Hero. Each has its own moods (the agent reads them with avatar info ), drawing and voice.

- Sound : chalk on slate as it writes, a bell for questions. The character's own voice speaks only when it needs you ("Done", "Your turn in the terminal"); "Speak on every mood", in the character gallery, makes it speak on every mood the agent gives it too. One button turns all sound off.

- Handwriting : six chalk-like fonts; Patrick Hand by default.

### When an agent says the command is not found

Some tools keep one background process alive and run commands through it: tmux, screen, or Codex's shared app-server. That process keeps the environment of the terminal it was first started from. If it was started outside More Space, it cannot see the command: restart it once from a More Space terminal (for Codex: codex app-server daemon restart , or run codex --no-daemon ). Started from any More Space terminal, it keeps working afterwards, even across windows and restarts: the command lives in a fixed folder and finds the window open on the project it runs in.

## Your data

Boards are kept per project folder in the app's own data folder (on macOS, ~/Library/Application Support/more-space/boards/ ), never in the project. Pinned images are copied there. Nothing leaves your computer, except an image the agent pins from a URL, which the app downloads.

## Platforms

macOS, Windows and Linux. The terminal runs your login shell on macOS and Linux, and PowerShell on Windows (PowerShell 7 when installed, otherwise Windows PowerShell). Git must be installed for the branch in the title and for the avatar's reactions to file changes.

## Development

Needs Bun .

bun install bun start # build and open (asks for a project) bun start -- --cwd=/path/to/project # open straight on a project bun run check # typecheck, tests, build bun run package # installable app for this system, in release/ bun run icon # regenerate icon files from assets/icon/icon.svg

The project name is defined once, in package.json ; the window title, the command, the socket variable, the data folder and the packaged app's name all derive from it.

See CONTRIBUTING.md for how to work on it, and how releases are made.
